questions.hint: Start at the left edge of the ruler (0 cm) and follow the ruler markings across to the tick mark directly below arrow a.

keyPoints.note: Read the centimetre number on the ruler scale directly underneath the tip of the arrow.
Look at the highlighted circle labeled a above the ruler and trace straight down to the number on the ruler.

questions.solution: Arrow a points directly to the \(2\) mark on the centimetre ruler, so the length is \(2\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Locate the starting edge of the ruler at \(0\text{ cm}\) on the far left and find arrow a (highlighted in yellow) above the ruler.

Find row b and trace the tip of pencil b down to the number on the ruler.

questions.solution: Pencil b starts at \(0\text{ cm}\) and its sharp tip aligns with \(8\text{ cm}\) on the ruler, so its length is \(8\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Check that the flat eraser end of pencil b is lined up with the \(0\text{ cm}\) start edge of the ruler (shown by the blue dashed line).

questions.solution: Pencil c starts at \(0\text{ cm}\) and its sharp tip aligns with \(10\text{ cm}\) on the ruler, so its length is \(10\text{ cm}\).

Find row f and trace the tip of pencil f down to the number on the ruler.

questions.solution: Pencil f starts at \(0\text{ cm}\) and its sharp tip aligns with \(12\text{ cm}\) on the ruler, so its length is \(12\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Check that the flat eraser end of pencil f is lined up with the \(0\text{ cm}\) start edge of the ruler (shown by the blue dashed line).

meta.question: 12f

questions.stem: Use the \(1\text{ cm}\) dot paper to make a line of length \(6\text{ cm}\). Since adjacent dots are \(1\text{ cm}\) apart, how many \(1\text{ cm}\) gaps and dots does a \(6\text{ cm}\) line span?

questions.hint: Each space between two neighbouring dots is 1 cm. Count the spaces (gaps), not just the dots: 1 gap connects 2 dots, so 6 gaps connect 7 dots.

keyPoints.note: The distance from one dot to the next dot is 1 cm (like one Base 10 unit cube).

questions.solution: Each gap between adjacent dots is \(1\text{ cm}\), so a \(6\text{ cm}\) line spans \(6\) gaps of \(1\text{ cm}\) and connects \(7\) dots from \(0\text{ cm}\) to \(6\text{ cm}\).

questions.hint: Each space between two neighbouring dots is 1 cm. Count the spaces (gaps), not just the dots: 1 gap connects 2 dots, so 10 gaps connect 11 dots.

keyPoints.note: The distance from one dot to the next dot is 1 cm (like one Base 10 unit cube).

questions.solution: Each gap between adjacent dots is \(1\text{ cm}\), so a \(10\text{ cm}\) line spans \(10\) gaps of \(1\text{ cm}\) and connects \(11\) dots from \(0\text{ cm}\) to \(10\text{ cm}\).

questions.stem: Using the leaf measurements from Question 9 (\(\text{a} = 2\text{ cm},\; \text{b} = 5\text{ cm},\; \text{c} = 3\text{ cm},\; \text{d} = 5\text{ cm},\; \text{e} = 10\text{ cm},\; \text{f} = 7\text{ cm}\)), what is the difference in length between the longest and the shortest leaf?
questions.hint: Find the longest leaf (\(10\text{ cm}\)) and the shortest leaf (\(2\text{ cm}\)), then subtract the shortest length from the longest length.

keyPoints.text: difference in length between the longest and the shortest leaf
keyPoints.note: Difference means subtract: Longest leaf (10 cm) − Shortest leaf (2 cm).

questions.solution: The longest leaf is leaf e (\(10\text{ cm}\)) and the shortest leaf is leaf a (\(2\text{ cm}\)), so the difference is \(10\text{ cm} - 2\text{ cm} = 8\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: Compare the six leaf lengths \((2\text{ cm}, 5\text{ cm}, 3\text{ cm}, 5\text{ cm}, 10\text{ cm}, 7\text{ cm})\) to find the longest leaf: leaf e is \(10\text{ cm}\).
Find the shortest leaf from the list: leaf a is \(2\text{ cm}\).
Subtract the shortest length from the longest length to find the difference.
The difference in length between the longest and the shortest leaf is \(8\text{ cm}\).

questions.stem: Use the letters a, b, c, d, e, f to place the real classroom objects from Question 11 (a: \(10\text{ cm}\) base-10 rod, b: \(16\text{ cm}\) envelope, c: \(6\text{ cm}\) eraser, d: \(3\text{ cm}\) paperclip, e: \(4\text{ cm}\) sharpener, f: \(22\text{ cm}\) shoe) in order of length from shortest to longest.
options: d, e, c, a, b, f
a, b, c, d, e, f
f, b, a, c, e, d
d, c, e, a, b, f
questions.hint: Compare the centimetre lengths \((3\text{ cm}, 4\text{ cm}, 6\text{ cm}, 10\text{ cm}, 16\text{ cm}, 22\text{ cm})\) from smallest to largest and match each length to its letter.

keyPoints.text: order of length from shortest to longest
keyPoints.note: Start with the smallest length (3 cm for d) and finish with the longest length (22 cm for f).

questions.solution: Ordering the lengths from shortest to longest gives \(3\text{ cm (d)}, 4\text{ cm (e)}, 6\text{ cm (c)}, 10\text{ cm (a)}, 16\text{ cm (b)}, 22\text{ cm (f)}\), which is d, e, c, a, b, f.

steps.explain: Find the two shortest objects first: the paperclip d (\(3\text{ cm}\)) is the shortest, followed by the sharpener e (\(4\text{ cm}\)).
Find the next two lengths in order: the eraser c (\(6\text{ cm}\)), followed by the base-10 rod a (\(10\text{ cm}\)).
Find the two longest objects: the envelope b (\(16\text{ cm}\)), and finally the shoe f (\(22\text{ cm}\)).
Write the letters in order from shortest to longest: d, e, c, a, b, f.

meta.source: Maths Plus 3 (Stage 2) Student Book · Unit 4: Measuring in centimetres

questions.hint: Start at Hockey on the map and use the compass rose (N = up, S = down, E = right, W = left) to look west (to the left).

keyPoints.text: Which town is west of Hockey?
keyPoints.note: West (W) points to the left on the compass. Start at Hockey and trace on the map.

questions.solution: Starting at Hockey and moving west leads to Cricket, so the answer is Cricket.

steps.explain: Check the compass rose on the left (highlighted in yellow) and locate the starting place Hockey on the Map of Sport Island.

keyPoints.note: East is to the right on the compass rose. Look directly to the right of Bear.

questions.solution: Looking east (to the right) from Bear at the top of Kangaroo Island leads directly to Monster Mountains.

questions.stem: Look at the seven angles labelled A to G. If you colour green all angles that are smaller than a right angle, which angles should be coloured green?

questions.stem: Look at the seven angles labelled A to G. How many of the angles are larger than a right angle?

keyPoints.note: Compare the amount of opening between the two arms of each angle to a square corner.

questions.stem: Which list names five everyday classroom objects whose corners form right angles?

Round clock face, basketball, globe, circular mat, and round waste bin
Open scissors blade tip, sharpened pencil point, slice of pizza tip, and traffic cone top
Curvedarchway, coiled spring, oval mirror, and beanbag

steps.explain: A **right angle** looks like the square corner of a sheet of paper (\(90^\circ\)), where a vertical edge and a horizontal edge meet.
